subject: This material is about how neurons communicate across chemical synapses, from the arrival of an action potential to the receptor effects and the clearing of the transmitter.

topics.title: What a synapse is, and the two kinds
points: A synapse is the junction where one neuron communicates with another cell, made up of the presynaptic neuron, the postsynaptic neuron and a synaptic cleft about twenty nanometres across.
Electrical synapses connect cells directly through gap junctions, are essentially instantaneous and bidirectional, but are fast and rare in the mammalian brain.

Chemical synapses use a neurotransmitter, have a delay of roughly half a millisecond, and go only one way from presynaptic to postsynaptic, and that unidirectionality is what allows circuits to compute anything.

topics.title: The sequence of transmission at a chemical synapse
points: An action potential arrives at the axon terminal and opens voltage-gated calcium channels, so calcium rushes in from outside where its concentration is far higher.

The calcium influx is the trigger that converts an electrical signal into a chemical one, causing synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter into the cleft by exocytosis.
The neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, producing a postsynaptic potential.

topics.title: Why calcium is the trigger, not the messenger
points: If you remove extracellular calcium, the action potential still arrives and the vesicles are still loaded, but nothing is released.
This shows that the calcium influx, not the action potential itself, is the step that actually triggers transmitter release.

topics.title: Ionotropic receptors
points: Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels where the receptor itself is the channel.
Neurotransmitter binding opens the pore directly, so ions flow within milliseconds and the effect is fast but short-lived.
The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is the classic example.

topics.title: Metabotropic receptors and second messengers
points: Metabotropic receptors are G-protein-coupled, not channels, and binding activates a G protein that starts a second messenger cascade.
The cascade can open channels elsewhere or change gene expression, so the effect is slower, hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, but longer-lasting.
The cascade amplifies the signal because one receptor activates many G proteins and each cascade produces many second messenger molecules.

topics.title: The transmitter is not what decides the effect
points: The effect of a neurotransmitter is determined by its receptor, not by the transmitter itself.
Acetylcholine is excitatory at the nicotinic receptor on skeletal muscle but inhibitory at muscarinic receptors in the heart, the same molecule acting through different receptor families.
There is no such thing as an excitatory neurotransmitter, only excitatory receptors, and this is a distinction students get backwards constantly.

topics.title: Postsynaptic potentials and how they sum
points: An excitatory postsynaptic potential is a depolarisation that brings the membrane closer to threshold, typically from sodium flowing in, while an inhibitory one is a hyperpolarisation moving it away, typically from chloride in or potassium out.
Neither potential alone fires an action potential; they are graded, decay with distance and time, and must summate.
Temporal summation is one input firing repeatedly in quick succession, spatial summation is several different inputs firing at once at different locations.
The decision point is the axon hillock, where the density of voltage-gated sodium channels is highest, and that is where an action potential fires or does not.

topics.title: Clearing the transmitter from the cleft
points: Reuptake pulls the transmitter back into the presynaptic terminal or into glia through transporters, which is how serotonin is cleared and the mechanism SSRIs block.
Enzymatic degradation breaks the transmitter down in the cleft, as acetylcholinesterase does to acetylcholine, and that enzyme is the target of nerve agents and of drugs used in myasthenia gravis.
Simple diffusion away from the cleft happens for every transmitter but is the main route for only a few.

topics.title: Synaptic plasticity: long-term potentiation and depression
points: Repeated strong stimulation can produce long-term potentiation, a lasting increase in synaptic strength, or long-term depression, a lasting decrease.
This plasticity is the cellular basis of learning and memory.
